title: Our heart is restless (Confessions 1.1)
hook: the pull that keeps you refreshing an empty feed: Augustine opens his book on it
tomorrow: how do you invite in someone who already fills the house?

segments.voice: A week of neighbors, then a new year. Muslim neighbors, with esteem. Greetings of respect at Diwali and Vesak. A courtyard for seekers. Unity, not sameness. A house with many rooms. And yesterday, primary source: the saints, in their own words.
screen: `WITH ESTEEM · THE COURTYARD · UNITY, NOT SAMENESS.` → `IN THEIR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Late at night, your thumb refreshes a feed with nothing new in it. Then another app. Then the fridge, then back. Nothing's wrong, exactly. Nobody needs you. Something just won't settle. Yesterday's question was what Augustine actually wrote first. Not his birthplace. Not his sins. His first words are spoken to God, in Pusey's translation: "Great art Thou, O Lord, and greatly to be praised." And a few lines later, the sentence about that thumb.
screen: `REFRESH. REFRESH. THE FRIDGE.` → `GREAT ART THOU, O LORD.` → `A SENTENCE ABOUT THAT THUMB.`

segments.voice: Here it is: "Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." Three pieces. Thou madest us for Thyself: before a word about sin or searching, Augustine starts with what people are for. Our heart is restless: not my heart. He doesn't keep the restlessness as his private flaw; he puts it in the plural, for everyone listening in. Until it repose in Thee: the restlessness has a direction. It isn't only a problem to fix; it's a pull toward something. His Latin word is inquietum, unquiet. And around the line, he asks a question that sounds backward: should a person call on God first, or know him first? He doesn't settle it neatly. He leans on a promise instead: those who seek the Lord will find him, and those who find him will praise him. So he reaches, and praises while he reaches. Something to tell a friend tonight: the Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes this very page where it describes the desire for God, the longing it says is written in the human heart. That's the shape of the whole Confessions: a restless man telling his life back to the one he was restless for.
screen: `THOU MADEST US FOR THYSELF.` · `OUR HEART, NOT MY HEART.` · `RESTLESSNESS IS A PULL.` · `CALL FIRST, OR KNOW FIRST?`

segments.voice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper and write down, in two or three words, the restlessness in you right now: an urge to check something, a want you can't quite name. Don't fix it or scold it; just let it sit on the paper while you rest. If you pray, you can hold that word up to God the way Augustine held his, as a direction and not only a problem.
Our heart is restless. Augustine's line from his first page: made for God, and unquiet until we rest in him.
Keep this one: restless until. The sentence doesn't stop at restless; it keeps going, toward rest. Good night, restless heart.
